newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Ex-Soviet Georgia can't afford breaks to investors.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Soviet Georgia can't afford breaks to investors.

text.p: Georgia's extremely low rate of tax collection makes it unable to offer tax holidays to foreign investors, an official at the International Monetary Fund said on Tuesday.
Hunter Monroe, IMF representative in the former Soviet republic, told a group of foreign businessmen attending an investment conference that tax collection rates were woefully inadequate.

"At eight percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in 1996, tax revenues in Georgia are the lowest of any republic in the former Soviet Union, and it may be the lowest tax revenue in the world," he said.
"The use of exemptions for investors has been widely abused. The government is not in a financial position to afford exemptions and incentives."
Georgia abolished incentives for foreign investors, who were previously exempt from most taxes, at the end of last year.
Monroe said the government had taken steps to redress the low rate.
"They're doing what they need to increase tax revenue," he said, referring to reforms in the tax service and tax code.
Finance Minister Mikhail Chkuaseli told the gathering the government planned to raise tax collection rates to 11.6 percent of GDP in 1997 and 13 percent of GDP in 1998.
The IMF is in the second year of a $246 million lending program to Georgia and has given general approval to the Caucasian state's reform programme.
